## 1. Narrative Arc

The story management tells has narrowed sharply over these three quarters — and that narrowing is itself the most important signal. Two or three years ago Gestamp sold itself as a structural grower: a supplier winning share through "outsourcing" (carmakers handing more stamping work to specialists) and riding the shift to heavier electric-vehicle structures. By the November 2025 call that growth language is essentially gone. Executive Chairman Francisco Riberas opens with "this year remained very challenging," and the entire pitch has become "increasing profitability without growth." He repeats almost verbatim across all three calls: the focus is "profitability and balance-sheet strength," not volume.

The single thread that strengthens across the quarters is the balance sheet. In November 2025 leverage was 1.6x net-debt-to-earnings (before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization — EBITDA); by the February 2026 full-year call it had fallen to 1.4x, which management called "the lowest since the IPO" (the 2017 stock-market listing). The Phoenix Plan — a restructuring of the loss-making North American operations — is the other consistent win: North American profitability climbed from a 7% margin in 2024 to 8.1% in 2025 and is tracking toward a 10% target for 2026.

What quietly dropped out: the China growth story. In November 2025 management spent real airtime on "more than 45% growth" with Chinese carmakers; by Q1 2026 China is described as down ~10% on volume and the region is a "clear underperformance." India replaced China as the designated growth market. ## 2. Claims vs Financials (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Profitability is improving" | Auto-business EBITDA margin rose 11.1% → 11.9% in 2025; Q1 2026 margin +52 bps year-on-year | **Holds** — margin gains are real and consistent |
| "Solid set of results" | Revenue −5.4% in 2025; net income fell 188M → 152M (−19%); EPS 0.33 → 0.27 | **Poorer than the words** — the bottom line is shrinking, not solid |
| "Lowest leverage since IPO" | Net debt fell to ~1.82B at year-end 2025… | **Holds at year-end, but watch the seasonality** |
| (same) | …yet net debt is back to **1.97B as of 31 March 2026** | **Important caveat** — the "all-time-low" figure is a December snapshot; debt swings up ~150M by Q1 on seasonal working capital. This is a meaningfully leveraged balance sheet, not a cash fortress |
| Free cash flow is strong | 2025 free cash flow EUR 249M reported (EUR 278M ex-restructuring), "more than guided"; Q1 2026 free cash flow was negative | **Holds, with seasonality** — cash generation is real but lumpy and back-half-weighted |
| Margin gains from operations | Q4 2025 EBITDA flattered by EUR 34M of one-off customer settlements; Q1 2026 net income flattered by a EUR 23M financing accounting gain | **Partly cosmetic** — a chunk of the recent "improvement" is non-recurring items, not clean operations |

The forensic punchline: this is a company defending profitability on a **falling revenue base**. Revenue peaked at 12.27B in 2023 and has fallen two years running to 11.35B in 2025. Earnings per share has compounded **down** about 8% a year over five years. Management's framing ("solid," "very good year") is consistently a half-step warmer than the trajectory deserves — not dishonest, but optimistic packaging of a business in slow decline. One genuine bright spot the numbers confirm: trailing-twelve-month diluted EPS has recovered to 0.31 (from the 0.27 fiscal-year figure) and the latest quarter's EPS jumped ~85% year-on-year, so the very recent earnings trend has turned up off a low base.

## 3. Tone & Confidence Trajectory

**Stable, and notably defensive throughout.** There is no offensive growth language left to lose — by November 2025 the tone had already settled into "manage what we can control: cost, flexibility, the balance sheet." Riberas is candid about the things outside his control: foreign-exchange (a ~EUR 334M revenue drag in nine-month 2025, and a stated EUR 1.5B revenue loss versus 2022 currency levels), weak volumes, scrap-metal prices. The confidence that remains is concentrated in two places — the Phoenix Plan and the leverage ratio — and on both, management has so far delivered what it promised. The language is consistent and unhurried across all three calls; there is no panic, but there is also no enthusiasm.

## 4. Guidance Credibility

**Medium-to-High, and this is the company's strongest suit.** The Phoenix Plan targets were set publicly and then hit: an 8% North American margin for 2025 was guided and delivered (8.1%) in a market that came in ~6% weaker on volume than assumed when the plan was launched. The 2025 free-cash-flow guide was beaten. Full-year 2026 guidance is concrete — auto-business EBITDA margin above 11.9% and North American margin above 10% — and Q1 2026 is tracking it. They under-promise on revenue (explicitly refusing to guide top line, "better to assume bad news") and deliver on margin and cash. That is a credible, if unexciting, posture.

## 5. Analyst Pressure Points

Three recurring pressure points, and management's handling of each:

1. **"What will you do with the cash now that leverage is at a record low?"** (BNP Paribas, February 2026). Riberas explicitly punted: "what to do in the future with that is something that is not now our first priority… today it's very early." He floated consolidation, opportunities, and "increase remuneration to shareholders" as possibilities — but committed to none. **This is the load-bearing question for any value thesis, and management refused to answer it.**

2. **Western-European underperformance** (ODDO, repeatedly). Management insists it is not losing share — blaming specific programs (a UK program in 2025) and offsetting with Eastern-European growth. Plausible, but the underperformance has persisted across multiple quarters.

3. **The EUR 34M one-off customer settlements** — analysts pressed on whether more are coming. Riberas declined to give detail but signalled "a little bit more in 2026," confirming these flatter near-term margins.

🔴 Revenue has fallen two consecutive years; EPS down ~8%/year over five years — the base is shrinking.
🔴 Altman-Z score of 1.2 sits in the statistical "distress" zone (a solvency screen; below ~1.8 is the warning band) — driven by thin margins and ~2B of net debt against a low-margin business.
🔴 Recent profit improvement is partly cosmetic (EUR 34M + EUR 23M of one-offs across Q4 2025 / Q1 2026).
🔴 EV-program write-downs in two straight periods show the EV-structure growth bet is misfiring.
🔴 The capital-return catalyst was explicitly deferred by management — "not now our first priority."

🟢 Phoenix Plan delivering on every milestone — North America margin 7% → 8.1% → tracking 10%.
🟢 Deleveraging is real (1.4x year-end, lowest since IPO) and free cash flow is positive and beat guidance.
🟢 Eastern Europe is a genuine bright spot — 15.2% EBITDA margin, the strongest region, growing on Turkey ramp-ups.
🟢 Scrap prices turned up in Q1 2026 after a punishing 2025, a tailwind for the recycling arm.
🟢 Q1 2026 organic sales outperformed the market by 2.3% — the first clear outperformance in the set.

## 7. Hidden Signals

The most telling shift is geographic: China moved from hero to problem child in two quarters, and the company is repositioning toward India and Eastern Europe — lower-cost, higher-margin footprints. Riberas now openly describes "year-after-year downsizing of our operations in Western Europe." Read between the lines and this is a company quietly shrinking its high-cost legacy base to defend margins — a rational but defensive posture that caps the growth ceiling. Second signal: the repeated, almost ritual insistence on "constructive customer negotiations" and tooling-payment collection as a profit lever. When a supplier's margin story leans on year-end settlements and collecting tooling money, the underlying operating leverage is thin. Third, and most important for governance: the founder family (the two Riberas brothers plus their holding company) controls roughly 70-75% of the shares. That single fact means no outside investor can force a sale, a break-up, or a large capital return — the cash-return decision rests entirely with a family that just said it is in no hurry.

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE — a competent, family-controlled cyclical defending profitability on a slowly shrinking revenue base, deleveraging steadily but with no committed catalyst to release the value.**

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a deep-value multiple (4.7x price-to-free-cash-flow) whose re-rating depends on a capital-return decision that a 70%+ controlling family has explicitly declined to make.** Without an activist (impossible here, given control) or a committed buyback/special dividend, the cheapness can persist indefinitely. The deleveraging is genuine and the operations are well-run, but a low multiple on a low-margin, FX-battered, slowly-declining auto supplier with distress-zone solvency metrics is exactly the profile that stays cheap.

On the economic moat: Gestamp has a **narrow** moat at best — scale and engineering know-how in hot-stamping and EV chassis give it some cost and switching-cost advantage with carmakers, but a 6.1% return on invested capital (below its likely cost of capital) and a gross margin contracting to 14.9% show the moat is not generating excess returns. This is an **eroding** position: returns and margins on the auto business are being defended by cost-cutting, not widened by pricing power. On secular threat: the structural risk is the long electric-vehicle transition reshaping vehicle architecture plus the rise of Chinese carmakers who increasingly localize their own supply — a **material** (not yet terminal) threat. Gestamp is adapting (EV chassis, door rings, Chinese-OEM wins), but the EV write-downs show the transition is a cost as much as an opportunity. The cheapness is best read as a **fear-print blended with a genuinely impaired growth profile** — not a clean mispricing, and not yet a terminal value trap, but closer to a value trap than to hidden upside given the controlled share register.

Three consecutive earnings calls are on the table: the nine-month 2025 update (November 2025), the full-year 2025 results (February 2026), and the first-quarter 2026 results (May 2026).*

## 1. Narrative Arc

The story management tells has narrowed sharply over these three quarters — and that narrowing is itself the most important signal. Two or three years ago Gestamp sold itself as a structural grower: a supplier winning share through "outsourcing" (carmakers handing more stamping work to specialists) and riding the shift to heavier electric-vehicle structures. By the November 2025 call that growth language is essentially gone. Executive Chairman Francisco Riberas opens with "this year remained very challenging," and the entire pitch has become "increasing profitability without growth." He repeats almost verbatim across all three calls: the focus is "profitability and balance-sheet strength," not volume.

The single thread that strengthens across the quarters is the balance sheet. In November 2025 leverage was 1.6x net-debt-to-earnings (before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization — EBITDA); by the February 2026 full-year call it had fallen to 1.4x, which management called "the lowest since the IPO" (the 2017 stock-market listing). The Phoenix Plan — a restructuring of the loss-making North American operations — is the other consistent win: North American profitability climbed from a 7% margin in 2024 to 8.1% in 2025 and is tracking toward a 10% target for 2026.

What quietly dropped out: the China growth story. In November 2025 management spent real airtime on "more than 45% growth" with Chinese carmakers; by Q1 2026 China is described as down ~10% on volume and the region is a "clear underperformance." India replaced China as the designated growth market. The EV-structure thesis also softened into a liability — 2025 and Q1 2026 both carried write-downs (EUR 52 million of asset write-downs in 2025, another EUR 15 million in Q1 2026) tied to customers slowing their EV roll-outs.

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |

| "Lowest leverage since IPO" | Net debt fell to ~1.82B at year-end 2025… | **Holds at year-end, but watch the seasonality** |

## 3. Tone & Confidence Trajectory

**Stable, and notably defensive throughout.** There is no offensive growth language left to lose — by November 2025 the tone had already settled into "manage what we can control: cost, flexibility, the balance sheet." Riberas is candid about the things outside his control: foreign-exchange (a ~EUR 334M revenue drag in nine-month 2025, and a stated EUR 1.5B revenue loss versus 2022 currency levels), weak volumes, scrap-metal prices. The confidence that remains is concentrated in two places — the Phoenix Plan and the leverage ratio — and on both, management has so far delivered what it promised. The language is consistent and unhurried across all three calls; there is no panic, but there is also no enthusiasm.

## 4. Guidance Credibility

**Medium-to-High, and this is the company's strongest suit.** The Phoenix Plan targets were set publicly and then hit: an 8% North American margin for 2025 was guided and delivered (8.1%) in a market that came in ~6% weaker on volume than assumed when the plan was launched. The 2025 free-cash-flow guide was beaten. Full-year 2026 guidance is concrete — auto-business EBITDA margin above 11.9% and North American margin above 10% — and Q1 2026 is tracking it. Against the screener's earnings-beat record of only 3 of the last 7 quarters (43%), the picture is mixed on headline beats but clean on the self-set operational milestones management actually controls. They under-promise on revenue (explicitly refusing to guide top line, "better to assume bad news") and deliver on margin and cash. That is a credible, if unexciting, posture.

## 5. Analyst Pressure Points

Three recurring pressure points, and management's handling of each:

1. **"What will you do with the cash now that leverage is at a record low?"** (BNP Paribas, February 2026). Riberas explicitly punted: "what to do in the future with that is something that is not now our first priority… today it's very early." He floated consolidation, opportunities, and "increase remuneration to shareholders" as possibilities — but committed to none. **This is the load-bearing question for any value thesis, and management refused to answer it.**

2. **Western-European underperformance** (ODDO, repeatedly). Management insists it is not losing share — blaming specific programs (a UK program in 2025) and offsetting with Eastern-European growth. Plausible, but the underperformance has persisted across multiple quarters.

3. **The EUR 34M one-off customer settlements** — analysts pressed on whether more are coming. Riberas declined to give detail but signalled "a little bit more in 2026," confirming these flatter near-term margins.

## 6. Red Flags / Green Flags

🔴 Revenue has fallen two consecutive years; EPS down ~8%/year over five years — the base is shrinking.
🔴 Altman-Z score of 1.2 sits in the statistical "distress" zone (a solvency screen; below ~1.8 is the warning band) — driven by thin margins and ~2B of net debt against a low-margin business.
🔴 Recent profit improvement is partly cosmetic (EUR 34M + EUR 23M of one-offs across Q4 2025 / Q1 2026).
🔴 EV-program write-downs in two straight periods show the EV-structure growth bet is misfiring.
🔴 The capital-return catalyst was explicitly deferred by management — "not now our first priority."

🟢 Phoenix Plan delivering on every milestone — North America margin 7% → 8.1% → tracking 10%.
🟢 Deleveraging is real (1.4x year-end, lowest since IPO) and free cash flow is positive and beat guidance.
🟢 Eastern Europe is a genuine bright spot — 15.2% EBITDA margin, the strongest region, growing on Turkey ramp-ups.
🟢 Scrap prices turned up in Q1 2026 after a punishing 2025, a tailwind for the recycling arm.
🟢 Q1 2026 organic sales outperformed the market by 2.3% — the first clear outperformance in the set.

## 7. Hidden Signals

The most telling shift is geographic: China moved from hero to problem child in two quarters, and the company is repositioning toward India and Eastern Europe — lower-cost, higher-margin footprints. Riberas now openly describes "year-after-year downsizing of our operations in Western Europe." Read between the lines and this is a company quietly shrinking its high-cost legacy base to defend margins — a rational but defensive posture that caps the growth ceiling. Second signal: the repeated, almost ritual insistence on "constructive customer negotiations" and tooling-payment collection as a profit lever. When a supplier's margin story leans on year-end settlements and collecting tooling money, the underlying operating leverage is thin. Third, and most important for governance: the founder family (the two Riberas brothers plus their holding company) controls roughly 70-75% of the shares. That single fact means no outside investor can force a sale, a break-up, or a large capital return — the cash-return decision rests entirely with a family that just said it is in no hurry.

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE — a competent, family-controlled cyclical defending profitability on a slowly shrinking revenue base, deleveraging steadily but with no committed catalyst to release the value.**

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is a deep-value multiple (4.7x price-to-free-cash-flow) whose re-rating depends on a capital-return decision that a 70%+ controlling family has explicitly declined to make.** Without an activist (impossible here, given control) or a committed buyback/special dividend, the cheapness can persist indefinitely. The deleveraging is genuine and the operations are well-run, but a low multiple on a low-margin, FX-battered, slowly-declining auto supplier with distress-zone solvency metrics is exactly the profile that stays cheap.

On the economic moat: Gestamp has a **narrow** moat at best — scale and engineering know-how in hot-stamping and EV chassis give it some cost and switching-cost advantage with carmakers, but a 6.1% return on invested capital (below its likely cost of capital) and a gross margin contracting to 14.9% show the moat is not generating excess returns. This is an **eroding** position: returns and margins on the auto business are being defended by cost-cutting, not widened by pricing power. On secular threat: the structural risk is the long electric-vehicle transition reshaping vehicle architecture plus the rise of Chinese carmakers who increasingly localize their own supply — a **material** (not yet terminal) threat. Gestamp is adapting (EV chassis, door rings, Chinese-OEM wins), but the EV write-downs show the transition is a cost as much as an opportunity. The cheapness is best read as a **fear-print blended with a genuinely impaired growth profile** — not a clean mispricing, and not yet a terminal value trap, but closer to a value trap than to hidden upside given the controlled share register.

# Forensic Dossier — Gestamp Automoción, S.A. (GEST.MC)

*A deep dive on management and the setup, built from three consecutive earnings calls (nine-month 2025 on 2025-11-04, full-year 2025 on 2026-02-26, and first-quarter 2026 on 2026-05-13) cross-checked against the hard financials from our screener.*

Gestamp is a Spanish auto-parts maker. It stamps and hot-forms metal into the structural skeleton and chassis of cars — the body-in-white and safety structures — and sells to nearly every major carmaker worldwide. It is a scale, low-margin, capital-heavy supplier riding on top of global car-production volumes, which have been flat-to-down in its core markets for two years.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has narrowed and hardened over these three quarters, and that is the single most important thing to notice. There is no growth story here anymore — there is a profitability-and-balance-sheet story.

At the nine-month 2025 call, the executive chairman, Francisco Riberas, still framed the year as "very challenging" but leaned on the idea that the company was "performing quite well year-to-date." The pitch was: volumes and foreign-exchange (the euro strengthening against the currencies Gestamp actually earns in) are hurting the top line, but we are lifting margins anyway through the "Phoenix Plan" — the restructuring of the loss-making North American operations. By the full-year 2025 call in February, the framing was explicit: "2025 has been another year of increasing profitability without growth." And by the first-quarter 2026 call, management had effectively stopped promising any revenue growth at all — "For this year, we don't see a growth... it is better for us now to assume that we need to focus in profitability and rather just to be waiting for volumes to come back."

The growth drivers that were once the Gestamp story — outsourcing gains (carmakers handing more stamping work to specialists) and content-per-vehicle growth — have been quietly dropped. A telling exchange came in February when an analyst from BNP Paribas asked directly about "the old Gestamp when we talk about the increase on growth above the market due to the increase of outsourcing... is this driver over?" Riberas did not defend the outsourcing thesis. He pivoted to "we have a very good position in the market" and "our market share remains quite intact" — a defense of the base, not a growth claim.

What replaced growth is a two-part self-help story: (1) squeeze more margin out of a flat or shrinking revenue base through cost flexibility and the Phoenix Plan, and (2) fortify the balance sheet — leverage cut to 1.4 times EBITDA (debt as a multiple of yearly cash earnings), "the lowest since the IPO," partly via a real-estate deal with Santander. The new, faint growth flicker is India and Chinese domestic carmakers, but management is careful not to oversell it.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Here the numbers and the story mostly agree — with one important tension around what "improving profitability" actually means for the bottom line.

**Trajectory: Stable, and consistently defensive.** Management's tone did not deteriorate across the three calls — but it never had an offensive gear to lose. From the first call to the last, the language is the language of a company managing a hard environment well, not one leaning into opportunity.

- Full-year 2025: "2025 has been a good year for Gestamp... marked by a complex context." The confidence is in execution (margin, leverage), never in demand.

3. **The €34M of customer settlements.** Analysts pushed on the one-off customer "compensation" payments (linked to carmakers cancelling electric-vehicle programs) and whether more are coming. Riberas declined to give segment detail — "I prefer not to provide you with data around what kind of customers or programs" — while hinting "there will be a little bit more during 2026." ## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Reported earnings power keeps falling.** Net income at a five-year low (€152M, down from €281M in 2023), EPS down ~8% a year over five years. The company is more profitable per euro of sales and less profitable in absolute terms.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most revealing shift is linguistic: management has stopped talking about **outsourcing-driven growth** — for years the core Gestamp bull thesis — and now talks almost entirely about **flexibility, cost, and Phoenix.** When directly handed the outsourcing question in February, Riberas did not reclaim it. **Trajectory classification: STABLE — a competently managed, structurally low-return cyclical, not a turnaround and not a decliner.**

The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position: **this is a cheap, cash-generative business whose cheapness is well-earned, not a mispricing waiting for a catalyst.** The free-cash-flow yield is genuinely attractive and the balance sheet is being repaired — but return on invested capital sits at 6.1%, below the cost of capital, and the one event that could force a re-rating (a shareholder-return program funded by the now-clean balance sheet) has been explicitly deferred by management. interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic dossier — Gestamp Automoción, S.A. (GEST.MC)

*Prepared 27 July 2026. Share price used throughout: €2.815 on the Madrid Stock Exchange (BME), the live quote on 27 July 2026. All figures in euros unless stated. Transcripts covered: 4 November 2025 (nine-month 2025), 26 February 2026 (full-year 2025), 13 May 2026 (first quarter 2026).*

Gestamp is a Spanish maker of the metal skeleton of cars — body panels, pillars, floors, chassis parts, door hinges — supplied to almost every major carmaker from plants sited next to their assembly lines. It is a scale business with thin margins, heavy machinery, and a controlling family that owns three-quarters of it.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

The story management tells has changed shape completely over these three calls, and the change is deliberate rather than cosmetic.

**Late 2025 — "we are performing well despite the market."** The November call framed everything as resilience against forces outside management's control: adverse currency moves, weak volumes in Europe, a China problem. The Executive Chairman, Francisco Riberas, led with revenue ("very close to EUR 8.5 billion") and only then with margin. Growth was still implicitly the destination; the weak patch was the detour.

**February 2026 — the pivot is stated out loud.** Asked directly by BNP Paribas whether the old outsourcing-driven growth engine was finished, Riberas answered without hedging: "we consider that it is better for us now to assume that we need to focus in profitability and rather just to be waiting for volumes to come back." He also declined to guide revenue at all — "we are not giving a clear guidance for that." That is the moment the company stopped being a growth story and started being a margin-and-cash story. The same call introduced the phrase that now anchors the whole thesis: "another year of increasing profitability without growth."

**May 2026 — the new story gets its first proof point.** The first-quarter call led with margin (11.0% in the car-parts business, up from 10.4%), with the North American turnaround, and with a claim that sales beat the market by 2.3% — the first outperformance in years. Revenue appeared fourth in the running order.

Two threads were quietly introduced and one was quietly dropped. Introduced: a geographic reallocation, away from Western Europe ("we are doing year after year some kind of downsizing of our operations in Western Europe") toward Eastern Europe, India, Morocco and Brazil. Also introduced: selling to Chinese carmakers as the replacement for lost European-brand volume in China. Dropped: any discussion of the outsourcing tailwind — carmakers handing more stamping work to suppliers — which was the original equity story at the 2017 listing and which the BNP analyst had to drag back into the room.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials

| Management's claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Increasing profitability without growth" (Feb 2026) | Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) margin: 10.9% in 2024 → 11.5% in 2025; the car-parts-only margin 11.1% → 11.9%. First quarter 2026: 11.0% versus 10.4%. Six consecutive periods of expansion. | **Holds.** This is the strongest, cleanest claim in the file. |
| "Solid results," "a good year" (Feb 2026) | Revenue fell for a third straight year: €12.27bn (2023) → €12.00bn (2024) → €11.35bn (2025). Both are true at once and management leads only with the first. |

See section 7. |

But global light-vehicle output fell 3.4% in the quarter with China down close to 10%, and China is precisely where Gestamp is under-exposed and had been losing. Excluding them the 2025 car-parts margin was 11.6%. | **Set against a flattered base.** Beating "11.9%" in 2026 requires roughly 30 basis points more underlying improvement than the headline suggests. |

**The divergence that matters most.** EBITDA margin is rising while operating margin and returns on capital are falling. Operating margin: 5.2% (2023) → 4.9% (2024) → 4.8% (2025). Capital spending runs about 7.5% of revenue and 1.10× depreciation — Gestamp is still investing above the rate needed merely to stand still. Return on invested capital of about 6% sits below any plausible cost of capital. The plain reading: the cost savings are real, but the machine eats them before they reach the owner.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising — but narrowly, and only on the things management now chooses to be measured on.**

- *November 2025 (defensive):* "So far, this year remained very challenging... adverse FX impact for us and also negative volumes in our core markets." The language is almost entirely about absorbing blows. Riberas volunteers a "huge underperformance in Asia of 12%."
- *February 2026 (defensive but resolved):* "For this year, we don't see a growth... we are assuming that the bad news are going to be there, and we are putting a lot of stress in the operations." Confidence has migrated from the top line to the cost line. Note the striking phrase on market share: "the answer is no. We are doing well with them" — an unhedged denial where a hedge would have been easy.
- *May 2026 (offensive, for the first time):* "we are now fully committed to achieve the full year '26 EBITDA margin of more than 11.9%," and on North America, "these results set the path to achieve the target of a 10% margin by end of the year." "Fully committed" and "clearly giving us the message that we are right on track" are new registers.

Specificity has increased, not decreased, on margin, leverage and restructuring — and has been withdrawn entirely on revenue. That is a coherent, honest trade: they guide what they control. The one place tone outruns evidence is the first-quarter outperformance claim.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High on what they guide. Low on what they do not.**

Every operational target set in these calls was met. The 2025 upgraded targets — margin, leverage, free cash flow — were all delivered ("Gestamp has met all the 2025 upgraded targets"). The Phoenix North American margin target of more than 8% was hit at 8.1% in a market 6% weaker than the plan assumed, which is over-delivery in substance. Leverage came in at 1.4×, better than the 1.5× promised at the 2023 capital markets day. Free cash flow beat.

Against that, the earnings line is a chronic disappointment. Across the last seven reported quarters the company beat the consensus earnings-per-share estimate three times (43%). That is defensible stewardship and a genuine warning to anyone underwriting earnings rather than cash.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**Deflected once, then deflected again — capital allocation.** BNP Paribas asked the obvious question in February 2026: leverage is at an all-time low, "what are you going to do with the cash?" The answer was a deferral: "what to do in the future with that is something that is not now our first priority... there will be opportunities to increase the remuneration to shareholders. But today, it's very early." Three months later the topic did not resurface. For a company whose entire remaining equity story is cash generation, this is the unanswered question.

**Refused outright — the composition of the one-off settlements.** Asked to split the €34m of customer compensation by division and to say whether more was coming, Riberas declined: "I prefer not to provide you with data around what kind of customers or programs or regions," while conceding "probably there will be more — a little bit more in the — during 2026." Analysts are being asked to model a margin that contains an undisclosed, management-timed component.

**Pushed on and later vindicated — Western European underperformance.** ODDO's Anthony Dick pressed in November 2025 on why the Western European shortfall was accelerating. Management redirected to China and to Eastern European offsets. Western European revenue then fell another 4% in the first quarter of 2026 and management confirmed it is deliberately shrinking the region. The analyst was right to keep asking.

**Asked but not answered — the shape of the recovery.** Nobody has been given a revenue trajectory, an order-book conversion schedule, or a view on when the roughly €1.5bn of cumulative currency-translation revenue loss since 2022 might reverse.

**What analysts are not asking, and should be.** Nobody on these three calls asked about the minority partners. Roughly €95m of the €247m of consolidated after-tax profit in 2025 belonged to partners in joint ventures, not to Gestamp's shareholders — and those partners sit disproportionately in the highest-margin regions. Nobody asked about receivables factoring either, despite the chief financial officer explicitly attributing weak first-quarter 2026 cash flow to "less factoring intensity."

**Red flag — the first-quarter outperformance framing (May 2026).** Presented as a competitive win; largely a China-underweight effect in a quarter when China fell 10%. Watch whether it survives a quarter in which China grows.

**Red flag — the guidance base is flattered (Feb 2026).** The 11.9% car-parts margin that anchors the 2026 target includes about 30 basis points of one-off program-cancellation compensation, with more of the same signalled for 2026.

**Red flag — capital allocation deferred with no date (Feb 2026).** Leverage at a post-listing low and the answer is "very early."

**Red flag — cash generation is thin against the asset base.** Capital spending absorbs 80% of operating cash flow. Peers in the same trade absorb 34% (Magna), 39% (OPmobility) and 56% (Martinrea). **Green flag — six consecutive periods of margin expansion on falling revenue (Nov 2025 through May 2026).** Documented, quantified, and achieved with disclosed mechanisms: flexibility measures, plant downsizing, and customer negotiations.

**Green flag — Phoenix delivered twice against a worse market than planned (Feb 2026).** North American margin 7.0% → 8.1% → 7.1% in the seasonally weak first quarter, tracking a full-year target above 10%.

**Green flag — the debt wall has been pushed out (Jan 2026).** The €1,700m senior facility was amended on 8 January 2026 to extend maturity from 2028 to 2031 at a lower cost, on top of €500m of senior secured notes issued in the second half of 2025. **Green flag — the controlling family is buying, hard.** The Riberas family's holding vehicle raised its stake to 75.301% — a record since the 2017 listing, when it held 71.271% — crossing that threshold on 10 April 2026 after buying from late February at prices around €3.12, about 11% above today's quote. **Green flag — bad news is disclosed early and precisely.** The €52m asset write-down, the €19m net negative at operating level, the €15m electric-vehicle program write-down in the first quarter of 2026, and the exact restructuring costs in both profit and capital spending are all volunteered, not extracted.

## 7. Hidden signals

**The Santander transaction is financing dressed as equity.** In July 2025 Gestamp agreed that a Santander vehicle, Andromeda Principal Investments, would invest €245.5m for minority stakes and preferred shares in four group companies holding Spanish real-estate assets, with Gestamp keeping full operational control. The proceeds cut reported net debt and delivered the 1.5× leverage promised at the 2023 capital markets day. Economically this is closer to a secured financing against property than to a partner sharing business risk — preferred shares carry a fixed claim. The chief financial officer described the improvement as "driven by our partnership with Santander" (Nov 2025) without characterising the instrument. Minority interest on the balance sheet jumped from €734m in June 2025 to €918m by September. Anyone reading the 1.4× leverage headline as pure operational deleveraging is reading it too generously.

**Terminology has shifted from "growth" to "flexibility."** Across the three calls the recurring nouns move from volumes, outsourcing and nominations to flexibility measures, efficiency, cost reduction, and constructive customer negotiations. "Constructive customer negotiations" appears in all three calls and is the euphemism for extracting compensation for cancelled electric-vehicle programs — a real cash inflow, but one that shrinks as the cancellations work through.

**The China story has been rewritten as a China-substitution story.** In November 2025 Riberas disclosed something genuinely useful and easy to miss: at the Edscha hinge business, "more than 30% of our sales are in China, and more than 50% of the sales of Edscha in China are to pure domestic Chinese OEMs," with third-quarter growth to Chinese carmakers above 45%. The old China business (supplying European brands there) is dying; a new one is being built underneath it. That is a real transition, not spin — but it is being executed inside a region whose reported revenue fell 9.5% in the first quarter of 2026.

**A succession signal outside the transcripts.** Spanish press reported the Executive Chairman appointing his daughter as an executive director. In a company where one family controls 75.3%, governance evolution is a live variable for minority holders and is not discussed on these calls at all.

**Free float is shrinking by design.** With the family at 75.301% and a Basque savings bank at about 3%, the tradable stock is roughly 21.7% of the company against a stated intention at listing of more than 30%. Average daily volume of about 290,000 shares means the entire float turns over roughly once every two years. Every family purchase makes the shares harder to own in size — and walks the register toward the thresholds where Spanish takeover rules make a delisting offer or a squeeze-out the natural next step. No such transaction has been announced; this is structural optionality, not a plan.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: turning (a genuine strategic pivot).** This is no longer the outsourcing-growth story that listed in 2017 and management has said so in plain words. It is now a margin, cash and deleveraging story executed on a shrinking Western European base, with growth capital redirected to Eastern Europe, India, Morocco and Brazil, and with the China business being rebuilt around domestic Chinese customers. The pivot is coherent, it is being delivered, and it has not yet reached the owner's line: revenue down three years, earnings per share down five, returns on capital still below the cost of capital.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the margin story — that is real and reasonably well understood by the fourteen or so analysts covering it. It is the capital structure. Against roughly €1.6bn of market value sit €1.98bn of net debt and €0.94bn of minority equity, and those minority partners took about 38% of consolidated after-tax profit in 2025 because they sit in the best regions. On the standard screen the shares look like 2.7× enterprise value to EBITDA; charge the partners properly and it is about 3.5×, against a live peer median near 4.4× on the same basis. The discount is real but it is roughly a fifth, not a half. Size this as a levered stub, where a single turn of multiple is worth about €2.28 a share in either direction — not as a cheap compounder.

**Economic moat: narrow, and stable rather than eroding.** The moat type is scale-cost with a switching-cost overlay. Gestamp's plants are co-located with customer assembly lines and its parts are designed into a specific vehicle program for that program's life, so displacement mid-cycle is rare; its hot-stamping and door-ring patch technology is a genuine technical lead, and it holds a five-year order book of roughly €47.5bn disclosed with the 2025 results. But the returns evidence forbids calling it wide: return on invested capital of about 6%, operating margin down three straight years, gross margin contracting. What stops the read at "eroding" is the countervailing evidence — the operating margin at the EBITDA line has expanded for six consecutive periods, Eastern Europe earns 15.2%, and management's flat denial of share loss in Western Europe has not been contradicted by the order book. The returns are being compressed by volumes, currency and relentless capital spending, not by a collapse in pricing power.

**Secular threat: manageable.** The obvious worry — electrification — does not apply here, and this is the most commonly mis-priced fact about the name. Gestamp sells the metal structure of a car: body-in-white, pillars, floors, chassis, hinges. None of it is a drivetrain part. Electric vehicles, being heavier, generally need more structural steel and more crash structure, and Riberas is explicit that "chassis for EVs, we are very much advanced and we're one of the leaders." The real structural pressures are the shrinkage of Western European vehicle production, which management is meeting by shrinking with it, and the transfer of global share to Chinese carmakers, which the company is meeting by selling to them directly. Neither impairs terminal demand for the product.

**So: is the cheapness a fear print or a shrinking base?** Mostly a fear print on a cyclical trough, with one honest caveat — the cash the business produces for its own shareholders, after partners and after the capital it must keep reinvesting, is thinner than the headline multiple implies. The shares are cheap; they are not as cheap as the screen says.

# Forensic dossier — Gestamp Automoción, S.A. (GEST.MC)

*Prepared 27 July 2026. Share price used throughout: €2.815 on the Madrid Stock Exchange (BME), the live quote on 27 July 2026. All figures in euros unless stated. Transcripts covered: 4 November 2025 (nine-month 2025), 26 February 2026 (full-year 2025), 13 May 2026 (first quarter 2026).*

Gestamp is a Spanish maker of the metal skeleton of cars — body panels, pillars, floors, chassis parts, door hinges — supplied to almost every major carmaker from plants sited next to their assembly lines. It is a scale business with thin margins, heavy machinery, and a controlling family that owns three-quarters of it.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

The story management tells has changed shape completely over these three calls, and the change is deliberate rather than cosmetic.

**Late 2025 — "we are performing well despite the market."** The November call framed everything as resilience against forces outside management's control: adverse currency moves, weak volumes in Europe, a China problem. The Executive Chairman, Francisco Riberas, led with revenue ("very close to EUR 8.5 billion") and only then with margin. Growth was still implicitly the destination; the weak patch was the detour.

**February 2026 — the pivot is stated out loud.** Asked directly by BNP Paribas whether the old outsourcing-driven growth engine was finished, Riberas answered without hedging: "we consider that it is better for us now to assume that we need to focus in profitability and rather just to be waiting for volumes to come back." He also declined to guide revenue at all — "we are not giving a clear guidance for that." That is the moment the company stopped being a growth story and started being a margin-and-cash story. The same call introduced the phrase that now anchors the whole thesis: "another year of increasing profitability without growth."

**May 2026 — the new story gets its first proof point.** The first-quarter call led with margin (11.0% in the car-parts business, up from 10.4%), with the North American turnaround, and with a claim that sales beat the market by 2.3% — the first outperformance in years. Revenue appeared fourth in the running order.

Two threads were quietly introduced and one was quietly dropped. Introduced: a geographic reallocation, away from Western Europe ("we are doing year after year some kind of downsizing of our operations in Western Europe") toward Eastern Europe, India, Morocco and Brazil. Also introduced: selling to Chinese carmakers as the replacement for lost European-brand volume in China. Dropped: any discussion of the outsourcing tailwind — carmakers handing more stamping work to suppliers — which was the original equity story at the 2017 listing and which the BNP analyst had to drag back into the room.

---

First quarter 2026: 11.0% versus 10.4%. Six consecutive periods of expansion. | **Holds.** This is the strongest, cleanest claim in the file. |

Capital spending runs about 7.5% of revenue and 1.10× depreciation — Gestamp is still investing above the rate needed merely to stand still. Return on invested capital of about 6% sits below any plausible cost of capital. The plain reading: the cost savings are real, but the machine eats them before they reach the owner.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising — but narrowly, and only on the things management now chooses to be measured on.**

- *November 2025 (defensive):* "So far, this year remained very challenging... adverse FX impact for us and also negative volumes in our core markets." The language is almost entirely about absorbing blows. Riberas volunteers a "huge underperformance in Asia of 12%."
- *February 2026 (defensive but resolved):* "For this year, we don't see a growth... we are assuming that the bad news are going to be there, and we are putting a lot of stress in the operations." Confidence has migrated from the top line to the cost line. Note the striking phrase on market share: "the answer is no. We are doing well with them" — an unhedged denial where a hedge would have been easy.
- *May 2026 (offensive, for the first time):* "we are now fully committed to achieve the full year '26 EBITDA margin of more than 11.9%," and on North America, "these results set the path to achieve the target of a 10% margin by end of the year." "Fully committed" and "clearly giving us the message that we are right on track" are new registers.

Specificity has increased, not decreased, on margin, leverage and restructuring — and has been withdrawn entirely on revenue. That is a coherent, honest trade: they guide what they control. The one place tone outruns evidence is the first-quarter outperformance claim.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High on what they guide. Low on what they do not.**

Every operational target set in these calls was met. The 2025 upgraded targets — margin, leverage, free cash flow — were all delivered ("Gestamp has met all the 2025 upgraded targets"). The Phoenix North American margin target of more than 8% was hit at 8.1% in a market 6% weaker than the plan assumed, which is over-delivery in substance. Leverage came in at 1.4×, better than the 1.5× promised at the 2023 capital markets day. Free cash flow beat.

Against that, the earnings line is a chronic disappointment. Across the last seven reported quarters the company beat the consensus earnings-per-share estimate three times (43%). The recent record: fourth quarter 2024 delivered €0.03 against €0.10 expected; fourth quarter 2025 delivered €0.08 against €0.10; first quarter 2026 delivered €0.087 against €0.085. The misses do not come from operations — they come from below the operating line: currency losses, rising interest expense, and the ever-growing depreciation charge.

There is no sandbagging pattern in the classic sense. There is something more subtle: management has progressively narrowed its promises to the metrics it reliably hits, and stopped commenting on the metric it reliably misses. That is defensible stewardship and a genuine warning to anyone underwriting earnings rather than cash.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**Deflected once, then deflected again — capital allocation.** BNP Paribas asked the obvious question in February 2026: leverage is at an all-time low, "what are you going to do with the cash?" The answer was a deferral: "what to do in the future with that is something that is not now our first priority... there will be opportunities to increase the remuneration to shareholders. But today, it's very early." Three months later the topic did not resurface. For a company whose entire remaining equity story is cash generation, this is the unanswered question.

**Refused outright — the composition of the one-off settlements.** Asked to split the €34m of customer compensation by division and to say whether more was coming, Riberas declined: "I prefer not to provide you with data around what kind of customers or programs or regions," while conceding "probably there will be more — a little bit more in the — during 2026." Analysts are being asked to model a margin that contains an undisclosed, management-timed component.

**Pushed on and later vindicated — Western European underperformance.** ODDO's Anthony Dick pressed in November 2025 on why the Western European shortfall was accelerating. Management redirected to China and to Eastern European offsets. Western European revenue then fell another 4% in the first quarter of 2026 and management confirmed it is deliberately shrinking the region. The analyst was right to keep asking.

**Asked but not answered — the shape of the recovery.** Nobody has been given a revenue trajectory, an order-book conversion schedule, or a view on when the roughly €1.5bn of cumulative currency-translation revenue loss since 2022 might reverse.

**What analysts are not asking, and should be.** Nobody on these three calls asked about the minority partners. Roughly €95m of the €247m of consolidated after-tax profit in 2025 belonged to partners in joint ventures, not to Gestamp's shareholders — and those partners sit disproportionately in the highest-margin regions. Nobody asked about receivables factoring either, despite the chief financial officer explicitly attributing weak first-quarter 2026 cash flow to "less factoring intensity."

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flag — the first-quarter outperformance framing (May 2026).** Presented as a competitive win; largely a China-underweight effect in a quarter when China fell 10%. Watch whether it survives a quarter in which China grows.

**Red flag — the guidance base is flattered (Feb 2026).** The 11.9% car-parts margin that anchors the 2026 target includes about 30 basis points of one-off program-cancellation compensation, with more of the same signalled for 2026.

**Red flag — capital allocation deferred with no date (Feb 2026).** Leverage at a post-listing low and the answer is "very early."

**Red flag — cash generation is thin against the asset base.** Capital spending absorbs 80% of operating cash flow. Peers in the same trade absorb 34% (Magna), 39% (OPmobility) and 56% (Martinrea). Gestamp's screen-cheap enterprise value against EBITDA is bought with the worst cash conversion in its peer group.

**Red flag — the equity is a thin slice of the enterprise.** Against a market value of about €1.60bn sit €1.98bn of net debt including leases and €0.94bn of minority equity. Debt and partners claim roughly two-thirds of the business; the listed shares are the leftover.

**Red flag — solvency scoring is weak.** An Altman Z-score of 1.2 (a bankruptcy-risk screen) is in distress territory, driven by a negative cash conversion cycle of −37 days: the company is financed by its suppliers (125 days of payables) and by factoring lines. That is efficient in calm markets and fragile in tight ones.

**Green flag — six consecutive periods of margin expansion on falling revenue (Nov 2025 through May 2026).** Documented, quantified, and achieved with disclosed mechanisms: flexibility measures, plant downsizing, and customer negotiations.

**Green flag — Phoenix delivered twice against a worse market than planned (Feb 2026).** North American margin 7.0% → 8.1% → 7.1% in the seasonally weak first quarter, tracking a full-year target above 10%.

**Green flag — the debt wall has been pushed out (Jan 2026).** The €1,700m senior facility was amended on 8 January 2026 to extend maturity from 2028 to 2031 at a lower cost, on top of €500m of senior secured notes issued in the second half of 2025. The refinancing risk that normally stalks a 1.5×-levered cyclical has been dealt with well in advance, and the accounting gain from that amendment (+€23m) is what lifted first-quarter net income.

**Green flag — the controlling family is buying, hard.** The Riberas family's holding vehicle raised its stake to 75.301% — a record since the 2017 listing, when it held 71.271% — crossing that threshold on 10 April 2026 after buying from late February at prices around €3.12, about 11% above today's quote. The screener's "insider buy ratio 0.00" is simply blind to Spanish regulatory filings; the best-informed holder in the security has been accumulating into weakness.

**Green flag — bad news is disclosed early and precisely.** The €52m asset write-down, the €19m net negative at operating level, the €15m electric-vehicle program write-down in the first quarter of 2026, and the exact restructuring costs in both profit and capital spending are all volunteered, not extracted.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The Santander transaction is financing dressed as equity.** In July 2025 Gestamp agreed that a Santander vehicle, Andromeda Principal Investments, would invest €245.5m for minority stakes and preferred shares in four group companies holding Spanish real-estate assets, with Gestamp keeping full operational control. The proceeds cut reported net debt and delivered the 1.5× leverage promised at the 2023 capital markets day. Economically this is closer to a secured financing against property than to a partner sharing business risk — preferred shares carry a fixed claim. The chief financial officer described the improvement as "driven by our partnership with Santander" (Nov 2025) without characterising the instrument. Minority interest on the balance sheet jumped from €734m in June 2025 to €918m by September. Anyone reading the 1.4× leverage headline as pure operational deleveraging is reading it too generously.

**Terminology has shifted from "growth" to "flexibility."** Across the three calls the recurring nouns move from volumes, outsourcing and nominations to flexibility measures, efficiency, cost reduction, and constructive customer negotiations. "Constructive customer negotiations" appears in all three calls and is the euphemism for extracting compensation for cancelled electric-vehicle programs — a real cash inflow, but one that shrinks as the cancellations work through.

**The China story has been rewritten as a China-substitution story.** In November 2025 Riberas disclosed something genuinely useful and easy to miss: at the Edscha hinge business, "more than 30% of our sales are in China, and more than 50% of the sales of Edscha in China are to pure domestic Chinese OEMs," with third-quarter growth to Chinese carmakers above 45%. The old China business (supplying European brands there) is dying; a new one is being built underneath it. That is a real transition, not spin — but it is being executed inside a region whose reported revenue fell 9.5% in the first quarter of 2026.

**A succession signal outside the transcripts.** Spanish press reported the Executive Chairman appointing his daughter as an executive director. In a company where one family controls 75.3%, governance evolution is a live variable for minority holders and is not discussed on these calls at all.

**Free float is shrinking by design.** With the family at 75.301% and a Basque savings bank at about 3%, the tradable stock is roughly 21.7% of the company against a stated intention at listing of more than 30%. Average daily volume of about 290,000 shares means the entire float turns over roughly once every two years. Every family purchase makes the shares harder to own in size — and walks the register toward the thresholds where Spanish takeover rules make a delisting offer or a squeeze-out the natural next step. No such transaction has been announced; this is structural optionality, not a plan.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: turning (a genuine strategic pivot).** This is no longer the outsourcing-growth story that listed in 2017 and management has said so in plain words. It is now a margin, cash and deleveraging story executed on a shrinking Western European base, with growth capital redirected to Eastern Europe, India, Morocco and Brazil, and with the China business being rebuilt around domestic Chinese customers. The pivot is coherent, it is being delivered, and it has not yet reached the owner's line: revenue down three years, earnings per share down five, returns on capital still below the cost of capital.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the margin story — that is real and reasonably well understood by the fourteen or so analysts covering it. It is the capital structure. Against roughly €1.6bn of market value sit €1.98bn of net debt and €0.94bn of minority equity, and those minority partners took about 38% of consolidated after-tax profit in 2025 because they sit in the best regions. On the standard screen the shares look like 2.7× enterprise value to EBITDA; charge the partners properly and it is about 3.5×, against a live peer median near 4.4× on the same basis. The discount is real but it is roughly a fifth, not a half. Size this as a levered stub, where a single turn of multiple is worth about €2.28 a share in either direction — not as a cheap compounder.

**Economic moat: narrow, and stable rather than eroding.** The moat type is scale-cost with a switching-cost overlay. Gestamp's plants are co-located with customer assembly lines and its parts are designed into a specific vehicle program for that program's life, so displacement mid-cycle is rare; its hot-stamping and door-ring patch technology is a genuine technical lead, and it holds a five-year order book of roughly €47.5bn disclosed with the 2025 results. But the returns evidence forbids calling it wide: return on invested capital of about 6%, operating margin down three straight years, gross margin contracting. What stops the read at "eroding" is the countervailing evidence — the operating margin at the EBITDA line has expanded for six consecutive periods, Eastern Europe earns 15.2%, and management's flat denial of share loss in Western Europe has not been contradicted by the order book. The returns are being compressed by volumes, currency and relentless capital spending, not by a collapse in pricing power.

**Secular threat: manageable.** The obvious worry — electrification — does not apply here, and this is the most commonly mis-priced fact about the name. Gestamp sells the metal structure of a car: body-in-white, pillars, floors, chassis, hinges. None of it is a drivetrain part. Electric vehicles, being heavier, generally need more structural steel and more crash structure, and Riberas is explicit that "chassis for EVs, we are very much advanced and we're one of the leaders." The real structural pressures are the shrinkage of Western European vehicle production, which management is meeting by shrinking with it, and the transfer of global share to Chinese carmakers, which the company is meeting by selling to them directly. Neither impairs terminal demand for the product.

**So: is the cheapness a fear print or a shrinking base?** Mostly a fear print on a cyclical trough, with one honest caveat — the cash the business produces for its own shareholders, after partners and after the capital it must keep reinvesting, is thinner than the headline multiple implies. The shares are cheap; they are not as cheap as the screen says.

Two corrections matter. First, those peer multiples exclude minority interests, as does the 2.7x the screen shows for Gestamp; but Gestamp's minorities are 21% of its enterprise value against roughly 6-14% at the peers. Put everyone on the same footing and the peer median is about 4.4x while Gestamp is about 3.5x -- a discount of roughly a fifth, not the half the raw screen implies. Second, and more important, the ranking inverts on cash: free-cash-flow yields run 24.9% at OPmobility, 24.1% at Martinrea and 15.6% at Magna against 12.8% at Gestamp, because Gestamp spends 80% of its operating cash flow on capital investment versus 34-56% at the others. It is the cheapest name in the group on EBITDA and the dearest on cash. Finally, this cohort de-rates together: European Tier-1 suppliers all move on the same unresolved drivers -- European vehicle output, tariff architecture, and now the oil shock -- so a good part of the gap to Magna is shared sector beta rather than anything specific to Gestamp. Only the leverage advantage (1.4-1.5x net debt to EBITDA against 2.7x at Forvia) and the six-quarter margin record are genuinely name-specific.
